claim: Over 600 proteins were identified in the secretome of murine visceral and subcutaneous white and interscapular brown adipocytes using BONCAT and mass spectrometry.
source: We employed bio-orthogonal non-canonical amino acid tagging (BONCAT) and mass spectrometry to comprehensively characterize the secretome of murine visceral and subcutaneous white and interscapular brown adip ocytes. claim: During 3 months of HFD, both AAV-eGFP and AAV-LRG1-FL groups gained an equivalent amount of weight to around 50 g.

claim: The AAV-LRG1-FL group had a dampened peak fasting glucose (LRG1: 225.9±6.5 mg/dL vs. eGFP: 263.7±10.8 mg/dL) at week 18.

evidence: The claim is supported by fasting glucose data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Glucose and insulin tolerance tests demonstrated that AAV-LRG1-FL mice had markedly improved glucose tolerance (p=0.0029).

claim: AAV-LRG1-FL mice had markedly improved insulin tolerance (p=0.023).

evidence: The claim is supported by ITT data shown in Figure 4M and AOC analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Glucose tolerance was significantly improved in the AAV-LRG1-FL group (p=0.020) without a significant difference in plasma insulin secretion during GSIS.

claim: Plasma non-esterified fatty acid (NEFA) levels were completely suppressed in both AAV-eGFP and AAV-LRG1-FL conditions during GSIS.
source: Glucose tolerance was significantly improved in the AAV-LRG1-FL group (p=0.020) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) without a significant difference in plasma insulin secretion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), and plasma non-esterified fatty acid (NEFA) levels were completely suppressed in both conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by NEFA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: HOMA-IR values trended lower in the AAV-LRG1-FL group, consistent with insulin sensitization.
source: HOMA-IR values trended lower in the LRG1 group, consistent with insulin sensitization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by HOMA-IR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I and represents an inference about insulin sensitivity.

claim: No significant difference was observed between AAV-eGFP and AAV-LRG1-FL groups in pyruvate tolerance test.

evidence: The claim is supported by PTT data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J.

claim: No significant difference was observed between AAV-eGFP and AAV-LRG1-FL groups in hepatic gluconeogenic gene expression.
source: To determine whether hepatic gluconeogenesis contributes to the difference in fasting glucose levels, we performed an oral pyruvate tolerance test (PTT) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J) and qPCR of hepatic gluconeogenic gene expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K) and observed no significant difference between the groups.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claim: LRG1 overexpression prevents obesity-related dysregulation of glucose homeostasis by insulin sensitization.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that LRG1 overexpression prevents obesity-related dysregulation of glucose homeostasis by insulin sensitization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing improved glucose homeostasis and insulin sensitivity.

claim: LRG1-KO mice were generated in B6 background using CRISPR-Cas9 targeting exon 2 of Lrg1.
source: To test whether LRG1 loss of function affects glucose homeostasis, we generated whole-body LRG1-KO animals in B6 background using CRISPR-Cas9 targeting exon 2 of Lrg1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim describes the method used to generate the knockout mice, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 targeting led to a frameshift mutation in Lrg1 and absence of LRG1 protein in plasma.
source: This led to a frameshift mutation in Lrg1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) and absence of LRG1 protein in plasma (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and western blot in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: LRG1-KO and WT littermate controls on HFD showed no difference in body weight.
source: LRG1-KO (Lrg1-/-) and WT (Lrg1+/+) littermate controls on HFD showed no difference in body weight (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D, E) or tissue weights at sacrifice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D, E.

claim: LRG1-KO and WT littermate controls on HFD showed no difference in tissue weights at sacrifice.
source: LRG1-KO (Lrg1-/-) and WT (Lrg1+/+) littermate controls on HFD showed no difference in body weight (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D, E) or tissue weights at sacrifice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue weight data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Male LRG1-KO animals demonstrated significantly higher fasting glucose levels compared to WT littermates throughout the HFD challenge (p=0.010).
source: Interestingly, male LRG1-KO animals demonstrated significantly higher fasting glucose levels compared to WT littermates throughout the HFD challenge (p=0.010) with a higher peak (KO: 261.6±11.3 mg/dL vs. eGFP: 225.0±10.9 mg/dL, mean ± SEM) at week 12 on HFD (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fasting glucose data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Male LRG1-KO animals had a higher peak fasting glucose (KO: 261.6±11.3 mg/dL vs. WT: 225.0±10.9 mg/dL) at week 12 on HFD.
source: Interestingly, male LRG1-KO animals demonstrated significantly higher fasting glucose levels compared to WT littermates throughout the HFD challenge (p=0.010) with a higher peak (KO: 261.6±11.3 mg/dL vs. eGFP: 225.0±10.9 mg/dL, mean ± SEM) at week 12 on HFD (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fasting glucose data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Fasting blood glucose levels are reciprocally regulated by LRG1 gain and loss of function.
source: Therefore, fasting blood glucose levels are reciprocally regulated by LRG1 gain and loss of function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that LRG1 overexpression lowers fasting glucose while LRG1 knockout raises it.

claim: GTT and ITT did not show significant differences between LRG1-KO and WT genotypes at the time points tested.
source: At the time points tested, however, GTT and ITT did not show significant differences between the genotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by GTT and ITT data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2H–K.

claim: B6 mice develop severe obesity upon HFD feeding but demonstrate only transient and mild hyperglycemia with moderate insulin resistance.
source: While B6 mice develop severe obesity upon HFD feeding, they demonstrate only transient and mild hyperglycemia with moderate insulin resistance (Winzell and Ahrén, 2004; Kleinert et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: db/db mice demonstrate hyperphagia and early-onset obesity, along with profound hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia due to a leptin receptor mutation and genetic background.
source: Due to a leptin receptor (Lepr) mutation and genetic background, db/db animals demonstrate hyperphagia and early-onset obesity, along with profound hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia (Kleinert et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge about the db/db model.

claim: Obesity and hyperglycemia over 400 mg/dL develop in db/db animals as early as 7 weeks of age.
source: We confirmed that obesity and hyperglycemia over 400 mg/dL develop in db/db animals as early as 7 weeks of age, while littermate misty mice with a WT Lepr gene (m/m) maintain fasting glucose levels below 200 mg/dL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight and glucose data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Littermate misty mice with a WT Lepr gene (m/m) maintain fasting glucose levels below 200 mg/dL.
source: We confirmed that obesity and hyperglycemia over 400 mg/dL develop in db/db animals as early as 7 weeks of age, while littermate misty mice with a WT Lepr gene (m/m) maintain fasting glucose levels below 200 mg/dL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by glucose data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: db/db mice showed higher circulating LRG1 levels compared to lean littermates.
source: Similar to B6 DIO mice, db/db mice showed higher circulating LRG1 levels compared to lean littermates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In LRG1-overexpressing db/db mice, there was 4.3-fold increased circulating LRG1.
source: In LRG1-overexpressing db/db mice, we confirmed 4.3-fold increased circulating LRG1 (Figure 5B, C) and that the adipose tissues were the major sites of Lrg1 overexpression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B and quantification in Figure 5C.

claim: The adipose tissues were the major sites of Lrg1 overexpression in AAV-transduced db/db mice.
source: In LRG1-overexpressing db/db mice, we confirmed 4.3-fold increased circulating LRG1 (Figure 5B, C) and that the adipose tissues were the major sites of Lrg1 overexpression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Starting 2 weeks post-injection, LRG1-overexpressing db/db animals demonstrated accelerated weight gain, such that by 10 weeks of age the LRG1 group weighed 19.6% more (p=0.004) than eGFP controls.
source: Starting 2 weeks post-injection, LRG1-overexpressing animals demonstrated accelerated weight gain, such that by 10 weeks of age the LRG1 group weighed 19.6% more (p=0.004) than eGFP controls (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: At week 6, glucose levels in the AAV-LRG1-FL db/db group were 33.6% lower than eGFP controls (eGFP: 399.5±31.7 mg/dL vs. LRG1: 265.4±19.6 mg/dL; p=0.0020).

source: Fasting plasma insulin levels were almost halved in the LRG1 group (eGFP: 12.5±1.3 ng/mL vs. LRG1: 6.3±0.6 ng/mL, mean ± SEM; p=0.0008) (Figure 5F).

claim: HOMA-IR was significantly lower in LRG1-overexpressing db/db mice.
source: HOMA-IR was significantly lower in LRG1-overexpressing mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).

claim: ITT profiles significantly differed between AAV-eGFP and AAV-LRG1-FL db/db groups (p=0.019).
source: Consistent with these findings, ITT profiles significantly differed between the two groups (p=0.019) (Figure 5G), largely due to differences in basal glucose levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITT data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: By 8 weeks of age, body weights continued to diverge between AAV-eGFP and AAV-LRG1-FL db/db groups, but no significant differences in fasting blood glucose or plasma insulin concentrations were observed.
source: By 8 weeks of age, body weights continued to diverge between the groups, but we no longer observed significant differences in fasting blood glucose or plasma insulin concentrations (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D–F.

evidence: The claim is supported by indirect calorimetry data and regression analysis shown in Figure 5H, I.

claim: There is a significant interaction effect between energy expenditure and body weight in db/db mice (p=0.0014).
source: Measurement of total energy expenditure (EE) across 5 days following acclimation (Figure 5H) and regression analysis against body weight using a generalized linear model using CalR (Mina et al., 2018) showed that there is a significant difference in EE between the two groups (p=0.0010) as well as a significant interaction effect between EE and body weight (p=0.0014) (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: LRG1 overexpression leads to a greater increase in energy expenditure per unit increase in body weight in db/db mice.
source: This suggests that LRG1 overexpression leads to a greater increase in EE per unit increase in body weight.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the regression analysis showing interaction between EE and body weight.

claim: Respiratory exchange ratio (RER) was higher in the AAV-LRG1-FL db/db group compared to eGFP controls (eGFP: 0.89±0.013 vs. LRG1: 0.93±0.014; p=0.046), suggesting a fuel preference for carbohydrates.

source: The eGFP group showed greater locomotor activity than the LRG1 group (eGFP: 234±17.5 vs. LRG1: 185±9.27, mean ± SEM; p=0.027), especially during the dark cycle (Figure 5L, M).
evidence: The claim is supported by locomotor activity data shown in Figure 5L, M.

source: Finally, LRG1-overexpressing animals had significantly greater food intake, consuming approximately 14% more food each day (p=0.039) (Figure 5N).
evidence: The claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: By week 10, eWAT and iWAT of LRG1-overexpressing db/db animals were 53% and 40% heavier, respectively, than those of eGFP controls.
source: Tissue weight measurements revealed that LRG1-overexpressing animals had accelerated gain of eWAT (p<0.0001) and iWAT (p=0.0001) mass, such that by week 10, their eWAT and iWAT were 53% and 40% heavier, respectively, than those of eGFP controls (Figure 5O, P).

source: We observed no difference in weights of BAT, liver, or gastrocnemius muscle (Figure 5O).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue weight data shown in Figure 5O.

claim: The AAV-LRG1-FL db/db group showed increased IRS-1 protein, especially in eWAT.

evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I and quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1J.

claim: qPCR analysis of hepatic gluconeogenic gene expression showed no significant difference between AAV-eGFP and AAV-LRG1-FL db/db groups except for Pck1, which was higher in the LRG1 group.
source: qPCR analysis of hepatic gluconeogenic gene expression showed no significant difference except for Pck1, which was higher in the LRG1 group (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1K.

claim: LRG1 overexpression elicits a constellation of metabolic effects in db/db animals that result in improved insulin sensitivity and WAT expansion-driven weight gain.
source: These results reveal that LRG1 overexpression elicits a constellation of metabolic effects in db/db animals that result in improved insulin sensitivity and WAT expansion-driven weight gain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the multiple experimental results showing improved insulin sensitivity and increased WAT mass.

claim: The distal portion of eWAT from B6 DIO mice was especially susceptible to CLS formation in eGFP controls, while the same region in LRG1-overexpressing animals displayed an 82% reduction in CLS number (p<0.0001).

claim: B6 iWAT contained fewer CLS compared to eWAT and did not show major morphological differences between AAV-eGFP and AAV-LRG1-FL groups.
source: B6 iWAT contained fewer CLS compared to eWAT and did not show major morphological differences between groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).

claim: In db/db eWAT, significantly reduced CLS were observed in the AAV-LRG1-FL group by 81% at week 7 (p=0.0001) and 85% at week 10 (p<0.0001).

claim: CLS in db/db iWAT from LRG1-overexpressing animals were reduced by 83% at week 7 (p=0.0043) and 88% at week 10 (p<0.0001).
source: CLS in db/db iWAT from LRG1-overexpressing animals were reduced by 83% at week 7 (p=0.0043) and 88% at week 10 (p<0.0001) (Figure 6C, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by histology images in Figure 6C and quantification in Figure 6E.

claim: Quantification of adipocyte cross-sectional areas in db/db eWAT slides showed significantly larger adipocyte size in the AAV-LRG1-FL group, especially at week 7 (p=0.0052).

claim: Liver sections from the B6 cohort showed a similar degree of steatosis in both AAV-eGFP and AAV-LRG1-FL groups, without any inflammatory lesions.

claim: Inflammatory foci in db/db liver were found only in AAV-eGFP-expressing animals.

claim: Inflammation is a key link between obesity and insulin resistance.
source: Inflammation is a key link between obesity and insulin resistance (Saltiel and Olefsky, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: The enrichment score for each of the top 20 immune-related pathways was negative in the AAV-LRG1-FL db/db group, indicating down-regulation of inflammatory processes.
source: The enrichment score for each of these pathways was negative in the LRG1 group, indicating down-regulation of inflammatory processes in these animals.

claim: GSEA of significantly regulated genes at the 10-week endpoint yielded similar down-regulation of immune-related pathways in the AAV-LRG1-FL db/db group.

evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claim: The AAV-LRG1-FL db/db group showed significant down-regulation of cytokines and chemokines such as Ccl3, Ccl4, and Cxcl9.

evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The AAV-LRG1-FL db/db group showed significant down-regulation of metalloproteinases such as Mmp12 and Mmp13 known to be highly expressed by macrophages.
source: Consistent with the pathway analysis, the LRG1 group showed significant down-regulation of cytokines and chemokines such as Ccl3, Ccl4, and Cxcl9; metalloproteinases such as Mmp12 and Mmp13 known to be highly expressed by macrophages; and various immunoglobulin subunit genes (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap data shown in Figure 6G and established knowledge about macrophage markers.

claim: CIBERSORTx estimated that the AAV-LRG1-FL db/db group contains fewer immune cells.
source: CIBERSORTx estimated that the LRG1 group contains fewer immune cells (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by CIBERSORTx deconvolution analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Macrophages were predicted to constitute the majority of immune cells in every db/db eWAT sample analyzed.
source: Macrophages were predicted to constitute the majority of immune cells in every eWAT sample analyzed, and the LRG1 group demonstrated a lower absolute quantity of macrophages (Figure 6H), without affecting their relative proportions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by CIBERSORTx deconvolution analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The AAV-LRG1-FL db/db group demonstrated a lower absolute quantity of macrophages without affecting their relative proportions.
source: Macrophages were predicted to constitute the majority of immune cells in every eWAT sample analyzed, and the LRG1 group demonstrated a lower absolute quantity of macrophages (Figure 6H), without affecting their relative proportions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by CIBERSORTx deconvolution analysis shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: At midpoint (week 7), the AAV-LRG1-FL db/db group showed 28–86% reduction of circulating chemokines such as MCP-1, MIP-1α, MIG, and IP-10 and cytokines such as TNFα and IFNγ.
source: We performed a multiplex cytokine assay to assess whether these differences are reflected in serum levels, and at midpoint (week 7), the LRG1 group showed 28–86% reduction of circulating chemokines such as MCP-1, MIP-1α, MIG, and IP-10 and cytokines such as TNFα and IFNγ (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiplex cytokine assay data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Many cytokine differences between AAV-eGFP and AAV-LRG1-FL db/db groups subsided by week 10, mostly due to a reduction of cytokine levels in the eGFP group.
source: Many of these differences subsided by week 10, mostly due to a reduction of cytokine levels in the eGFP group (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiplex cytokine assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: LRG1 overexpression attenuated pro-inflammatory processes associated with obesity.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that LRG1 overexpression attenuated pro-inflammatory processes associated with obesity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the multiple experimental results showing reduced inflammation markers.

claim: LRG1 contains leucine-rich repeat (LRR) domains, which form a structural framework for protein-protein interactions.
source: LRG1 contains leucine-rich repeat (LRR) domains, which form a structural framework for protein-protein interactions.
evidence: The claim represents established structural knowledge about LRR domains.

claim: Cytochrome c is released into the extracellular space following cell death.
source: In addition to its role in the respiratory chain and intrinsic apoptosis pathway, Cyt c is released into the extracellular space following cell death (Jemmerson et al., 2002; Renz et al., 2001) and mediates pro-inflammatory signals as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) (Grazioli and Pugin, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Extracellular cytochrome c mediates pro-inflammatory signals as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP).
source: In addition to its role in the respiratory chain and intrinsic apoptosis pathway, Cyt c is released into the extracellular space following cell death (Jemmerson et al., 2002; Renz et al., 2001) and mediates pro-inflammatory signals as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) (Grazioli and Pugin, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Binding between LRG1 and extracellular Cyt c has been shown to reduce apoptosis of lymphocytes and cancer cells in vitro.
source: Binding between LRG1 and extracellular Cyt c has been shown to reduce apoptosis of lymphocytes and cancer cells in vitro (Codina et al., 2010; Jemmerson et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The in vivo biological context and effect of LRG1-Cyt c interaction have remained unknown prior to this study.
source: However, the in vivo biological context and effect of this interaction have remained unknown.
evidence: The claim represents the authors' assessment of the novelty of their work.

claim: Adipocyte death in obesity is a key event promoting macrophage infiltration and WAT inflammation.
source: Adipocyte death in obesity is a key event promoting macrophage infiltration and WAT inflammation (Cinti et al., 2005), but the exact triggers of metabolic inflammation remain unidentified.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The exact triggers of metabolic inflammation remain unidentified.
source: Adipocyte death in obesity is a key event promoting macrophage infiltration and WAT inflammation (Cinti et al., 2005), but the exact triggers of metabolic inflammation remain unidentified.
evidence: The claim represents the authors' assessment of the current state of knowledge.

claim: LRG1-FL and Cyt c were successfully co-immunoprecipitated from the serum of db/db animals transduced with AAV-LRG1-FL, indicating the two proteins circulate as a complex.
source: In the serum of db/db animals transduced with AAV-LRG1-FL, we were able to successfully co-IP both LRG1-FL and Cyt c from the serum, indicating the two proteins indeed circulate as a complex (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Elevated Cyt c levels in circulation have been observed in conditions involving cell death or inflammation.
source: While elevated Cyt c levels in circulation have been observed in conditions involving cell death or inflammation (Adachi et al., 2004; Alleyne et al., 2001; Barczyk et al., 2005; Ben-Ari et al., 2003), it is not known whether obesity is associated with increased serum Cyt c levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: It is not known whether obesity is associated with increased serum Cyt c levels prior to this study.
source: While elevated Cyt c levels in circulation have been observed in conditions involving cell death or inflammation (Adachi et al., 2004; Alleyne et al., 2001; Barczyk et al., 2005; Ben-Ari et al., 2003), it is not known whether obesity is associated with increased serum Cyt c levels.
evidence: The claim represents the authors' assessment of the novelty of their findings.

claim: Western blot analysis of serum revealed that Cyt c is increased in db/db animals compared to lean littermates.
source: Western blot analysis of serum revealed that Cyt c is increased in db/db animals compared to lean littermates (Figure 7B, quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B and quantification in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Extracellular Cyt c levels trended higher at 7 than at 10 weeks of age in db/db mice, correlating with the time point when LRG1 overexpression has a potent physiological effect.
source: Interestingly, extracellular Cyt c levels trended higher at 7 than at 10 weeks of age (Figure 7B, quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), correlating with the time point when LRG1 overexpression has a potent physiological effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and represents an inference about the correlation.

claim: In B6 mice, HFD led to increased serum Cyt c levels.
source: In B6 mice, HFD led to increased serum Cyt c levels (Figure 7C, quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), and the trend continued at 15 weeks on HFD (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7C and quantification in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In CM of SubQ adipocytes treated with staurosporine (STS) for 24 hr, a robust increase in Cyt c was detected compared to vehicle controls.
source: In CM of SubQ adipocytes treated with staurosporine (STS) for 24 hr, we detected a robust increase in Cyt c compared to vehicle controls (Figure 7D, quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7D and quantification in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CM collected from adipocytes incubated in hypoxic conditions showed increased Cyt c compared to normoxic controls.
source: CM collected from adipocytes incubated in hypoxic conditions or treated with TNFα also showed increased Cyt c compared to normoxic or vehicle controls, respectively (Figure 7D, quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7D and quantification in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CM collected from adipocytes treated with TNFα showed increased Cyt c compared to vehicle controls.
source: CM collected from adipocytes incubated in hypoxic conditions or treated with TNFα also showed increased Cyt c compared to normoxic or vehicle controls, respectively (Figure 7D, quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7D and quantification in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Interstitial fluid (ISF) from eWAT and iWAT of B6 mice showed higher Cyt c levels in HFD-fed mice.
source: We next collected interstitial fluid (ISF) from eWAT and iWAT of B6 mice and found higher Cyt c levels in HFD-fed mice (Figure 7E, quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F), suggesting adipose tissues are a source of elevated circulating Cyt c in DIO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7E and quantification in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Adipose tissues are a source of elevated circulating Cyt c in DIO mice.
source: We next collected interstitial fluid (ISF) from eWAT and iWAT of B6 mice and found higher Cyt c levels in HFD-fed mice (Figure 7E, quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F), suggesting adipose tissues are a source of elevated circulating Cyt c in DIO mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of increased Cyt c in adipose tissue ISF.

claim: Extracellular Cyt c has been shown to exert a pro-inflammatory effect by acting on the toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)-mediated innate immune signaling pathway in astrocytes.
source: Extracellular Cyt c has been shown to exert a pro-inflammatory effect by acting on the toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)-mediated innate immune signaling pathway in astrocytes (Wenzel et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Circulating monocytes contribute to adipose tissue macrophages in obesity.
source: Because circulating monocytes contribute to adipose tissue macrophages in obesity (Oh et al., 2012), we tested whether bone-marrow derived macrophages (BMDMs) respond to extracellular Cyt c by upregulating pro-inflammatory genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Treating BMDMs with horse Cyt c led to >30-fold induction of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-responsive pro-inflammatory genes such as Il1b, Cxcl10, Il6, and Nos2 (p<0.0001).
source: Treating BMDMs with horse Cyt c led to >30-fold induction of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-responsive pro-inflammatory genes such as Il1b, Cxcl10, Il6, and Nos2 (p<0.0001), while pre-treatment of macrophages with a small molecule TLR4 inhibitor, TAK-242, prevented this induction (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Pre-treatment of macrophages with a small molecule TLR4 inhibitor, TAK-242, prevented Cyt c-induced induction of pro-inflammatory genes.
source: Treating BMDMs with horse Cyt c led to >30-fold induction of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-responsive pro-inflammatory genes such as Il1b, Cxcl10, Il6, and Nos2 (p<0.0001), while pre-treatment of macrophages with a small molecule TLR4 inhibitor, TAK-242, prevented this induction (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Cyt c in the extracellular space acts as a DAMP that activates innate immune signaling and polarizes macrophages into a more pro-inflammatory state.
source: These data confirm that Cyt c in the extracellular space acts as a DAMP that activates innate immune signaling and polarizes macrophages into a more pro-inflammatory state.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing Cyt c-induced pro-inflammatory gene expression.

claim: Co-treatment with rhLRG1 significantly dampened Cyt c-mediated induction of Il1b (P<0.0001), Cxcl10 (P=0.024), and Il6 (P=0.0008) in BMDMs.
source: Compared to single treatment, co-treatment with rhLRG1 significantly dampened Cyt c-mediated induction of Il1b (P<0.0001), Cxcl10 (P=0.024), and Il6 (P=0.0008), while Nos2 induction was not affected by co-treatment with rhLRG1 (Figure 7G).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Nos2 induction was not affected by co-treatment with rhLRG1 in BMDMs.
source: Compared to single treatment, co-treatment with rhLRG1 significantly dampened Cyt c-mediated induction of Il1b (P<0.0001), Cxcl10 (P=0.024), and Il6 (P=0.0008), while Nos2 induction was not affected by co-treatment with rhLRG1 (Figure 7G).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Pre-treatment of BMDMs with rhLRG1 followed by addition of Cyt c did not attenuate the latter's pro-inflammatory effect, suggesting that Cyt c-LRG1 complex formation is necessary for LRG1's modulatory effect.
source: Interestingly, pre-treatment of BMDMs with rhLRG1 followed by addition of Cyt c did not attenuate the latter's pro-inflammatory effect, suggesting that Cyt c-LRG1 complex formation is necessary for LRG1's modulatory effect (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G and represents an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Expression of alternatively activated (M2) macrophage markers was not affected by co-treatment with Cyt c and rhLRG1.
source: Expression of alternatively activated (M2) macrophage markers was not affected by co-treatment with Cyt c and rhLRG1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Western blot of db/db eWAT showed reduction of cleaved Caspase-3 in the AAV-LRG1-FL group, suggesting reduction of apoptotic cells with LRG1 overexpression.
source: We next explored if this immunomodulatory role of LRG1 can in turn reduce adipose tissue damage. Western blot of db/db eWAT showed reduction of cleaved Caspase-3 in the LRG1 group (Figure 7H), suggesting reduction of apoptotic cells with LRG1 overexpression.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7H and represents an inference about apoptosis.

claim: Decreased release of Cyt c into the ISF of eWAT and liver was observed in AAV-LRG1-FL db/db mice, consistent with lower circulating Cyt c detected in the serum.
source: We also observed decreased release of Cyt c into the ISF of eWAT and liver (Figure 7I), consistent with lower circulating Cyt c detected in the serum (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7I and Figure 7A.

claim: LRG1 can modulate the pro-inflammatory gene expression responses induced by Cyt c and subsequently reduce tissue damage and cell death.
source: Taken together, these results suggest LRG1 can modulate the pro-inflammatory gene expression responses induced by Cyt c and subsequently reduce tissue damage and cell death.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the multiple experimental results showing LRG1's effects on inflammation and cell death.

claim: Cyt c is a small (12.5 kDa), globular protein with a short half-life in circulation.
source: Cyt c is a small (12.5 kDa), globular protein with a short half-life in circulation (Radhakrishnan et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Small proteins such as Cyt c are expected to be rapidly cleared via glomerular filtration in the kidney.
source: Small proteins such as Cyt c are expected to be rapidly cleared via glomerular filtration in the kidney.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about renal clearance of small proteins.

claim: Much of extracellular Cyt c circulates as a complex with LRG1.
source: With the tight binding interaction between LRG1 and Cyt c, we hypothesized that much of extracellular Cyt c circulates as a complex with LRG1.
evidence: The claim represents a hypothesis based on the observed binding interaction.

claim: LRG1-KO animals almost completely cleared Cyt c by 2 hr after retroorbital injection, whereas in WT animals, an initial decrease in Cyt c was followed by nearly constant levels between 1 and 6 hr post-injection.
source: Plasma western blot showed that LRG1-KO animals almost completely cleared Cyt c by 2 hr, whereas in WT animals, an initial decrease in Cyt c was followed by nearly constant levels between 1 and 6 hr post-injection (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Fitting one-phase decay functions to relative Cyt c intensities showed that while both WT and LRG1-KO curves have similar half-lives (WT: 16.10 min vs. KO: 17.32 min), the WT trace plateaus at 0.2791, whereas the LRG1-KO curve approaches zero.
source: Fitting one-phase decay functions to relative Cyt c intensities showed that while both WT and LRG1-KO curves have similar half-lives (WT: 16.10 min vs. KO: 17.32 min), the WT trace plateaus at 0.2791, whereas the LRG1-KO curve approaches zero (Figure 7—figure supplement 1J, K).
evidence: The claim is supported by curve fitting analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1J, K.

claim: Appearance of Cyt c in the urine was observed as soon as 30 min after the injection, demonstrating that clearance of excess Cyt c is through the kidneys.
source: Concomitantly, appearance of Cyt c in the urine was observed as soon as 30 min after the injection, demonstrating that clearance of excess Cyt c is indeed through the kidneys (Figure 7—figure supplement 1L, M).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1L and quantification in Figure 7—figure supplement 1M.

claim: Urine Ponceau S staining showed that detected proteins were all below 25 kDa, the apparent size limit for urinary excretion.
source: Urine Ponceau S staining showed that detected proteins were all below 25 kDa, the apparent size limit for urinary excretion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ponceau S staining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1L.

claim: In LRG1-KO animals, Cyt c circulates as an unbound, free form that can be rapidly excreted by glomerular filtration, whereas the presence of LRG1 in WT animals prevents a portion of Cyt c from excretion due to formation of a complex larger than the size cutoff for glomerular filtration.
source: We reasoned that in LRG1-KO animals, Cyt c circulates as an unbound, free form that can be rapidly excreted by glomerular filtration, whereas the presence of LRG1 in WT animals prevents a portion of Cyt c from excretion due to formation of a complex larger than the size cutoff for glomerular filtration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the clearance data and represents the authors' mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Endogenous Cyt c was virtually undetectable in the serum of HFD-fed LRG1-KO mice.
source: Indeed, endogenous Cyt c was virtually undetectable in the serum of HFD-fed LRG1-KO mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1N.

claim: Cyt c is a native ligand of LRG1.
source: Taken together, these data directly demonstrate that Cyt c is a native ligand of LRG1, and that this interaction suppresses the pro-inflammatory effect of extracellular Cyt c and cell death (Figure 7J).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the multiple experimental results showing LRG1-Cyt c binding and functional effects.

claim: The LRG1-Cyt c interaction suppresses the pro-inflammatory effect of extracellular Cyt c and cell death.
source: Taken together, these data directly demonstrate that Cyt c is a native ligand of LRG1, and that this interaction suppresses the pro-inflammatory effect of extracellular Cyt c and cell death (Figure 7J).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the multiple experimental results showing functional effects of LRG1-Cyt c interaction.
